articles.label: County Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M reserves could vanish by 2028. Commissioners keep spending anyway.
articles.dek: A Flightline review of budget documents shows the county burned through $12 million in reserves last fiscal year alone. With hurricane season here and no plan to rebuild the cushion, what happens when the next storm hits?
brief: Escambia County's general fund reserves dropped from $59 million to $47 million in fiscal year 2025, according to budget documents reviewed by The Flightline.
At current spending rates, the county's rainy day fund could fall below the state-recommended minimum by 2028, leaving little cushion for hurricane response or economic downturns.
County commissioners have approved several large expenditures this year without identifying offsetting revenue or cuts to rebuild reserves.
articles.body:
The chart on page 47 of Escambia County's adopted budget tells the story in a single downward line.

General fund reserves stood at $59 million at the start of fiscal year 2025. By September 30, they had dropped to $47 million. The $12 million drawdown—roughly 20 percent of the county's savings—funded everything from employee raises to infrastructure repairs to a sheriff's budget that grew faster than tax revenue.

Now, nine months into the current fiscal year, county staff project another $8 million deficit. If that holds, reserves will drop to $39 million by October. Another similar year puts them at $31 million. By 2028, the county could fall below the 16.7 percent reserve threshold that the Government Finance Officers Association recommends as a minimum—roughly two months of operating expenses.

Hurricane season started June 1.

The math doesn't work

County Administrator Wes Moreno acknowledged the trajectory in a May budget workshop but stopped short of calling it a crisis.

"We're managing through a period of significant cost pressures," Moreno told commissioners. "Inflation, insurance, personnel costs—they've all outpaced revenue growth. That's not unique to Escambia County."

He's right that it isn't unique. But Escambia County faces risks that Duval or Hillsborough don't. The county sits on a coast that has taken direct hits from hurricanes in 2004, 2020 and 2024. Federal reimbursements for storm damage typically take years to arrive. Local governments need cash on hand to clear debris, repair infrastructure and keep services running while waiting for FEMA checks.

After Hurricane Sally in 2020, Escambia County fronted more than $40 million in emergency expenses. Some of that money still hasn't been reimbursed. After Hurricane Helene grazed the coast in 2024, emergency costs ran to $6 million. The county absorbed most of it from reserves.

Budget documents show the county has not established a dedicated hurricane reserve fund. The general fund balance serves as the de facto emergency cushion, the same pot that covers budget shortfalls, capital projects and unexpected expenses.

Spending continues

Despite the shrinking balance, commissioners have approved several large expenditures in recent months without identifying new revenue or offsetting cuts.

In February, the board voted 4-1 to allocate $3.2 million for a new emergency operations center generator system, drawing from reserves. In April, commissioners approved a $1.8 million contract for consulting services related to the county's comprehensive plan update. In May, the sheriff's office received a mid-year budget amendment adding 12 positions at an annualized cost of $1.4 million.

Each expenditure had its own rationale. The generator system replaced equipment that failed during a 2025 power outage. The comprehensive plan hasn't been updated since 2018. The sheriff cited rising call volumes and officer burnout.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, the lone no vote on the generator funding, has raised concerns about the spending pattern repeatedly.

"I'm not saying any of these are bad projects," Bergosh said during the February meeting. "I'm saying we can't keep doing this without a plan to rebuild the reserves. Every dollar we spend now is a dollar we won't have when the next storm hits."

His colleagues have not disagreed publicly. They've just kept voting yes.

Revenue options are limited

Escambia County operates under Florida's property tax caps, which limit annual assessment increases to 3 percent for homesteaded properties regardless of market value changes. The county's millage rate sits at 8.15 mills, below the 10-mill statutory cap but high enough that commissioners have shown little appetite for increases.

Sales tax revenue, the county's other major source, has grown modestly but not enough to keep pace with expenses. Tourism taxes flow to the Tourist Development Council, not the general fund. Impact fees from new development help fund infrastructure but can't legally cover operating costs.

Moreno has proposed a "sustainability plan" that would slow the reserve decline through a combination of modest fee increases, deferred capital projects and natural attrition in the workforce. He presented the framework at the May workshop but provided few specifics.

"We're working on the details," he said. "We'll have more to share during the budget hearings in September."

September is two months into hurricane season.

What the state recommends

The Florida Legislature doesn't mandate a specific reserve level for counties, but the GFOA's two-month recommendation has become the de facto standard. For Escambia County, that works out to roughly $35 million based on current operating expenses.

At projected drawdown rates, the county crosses that threshold in late 2027 or early 2028. If a major hurricane hits before then—or if any other large unplanned expense emerges—the timeline accelerates.

County Finance Director Sarah Faircloth noted in budget documents that reserves remain "adequate" under current conditions. The word "adequate" appears three times in the fiscal year 2026 budget summary. The word "plan" to rebuild reserves appears zero times.

The board's next budget workshop is scheduled for August 12. Public hearings on the proposed fiscal year 2027 budget will follow in September. Hurricane season runs through November 30.

The line on page 47 keeps pointing down.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The West Cervantes corridor was supposed to transform. Five years later, it's still waiting.
articles.dek: Millions in CRA funds, a Complete Streets redesign, and promises of revitalization. But between Graffiti Bridge and I-110, the vacant lots and shuttered businesses tell a different story.
brief: The West Cervantes Community Redevelopment Area has spent $4.2 million since 2021 with minimal visible commercial development
A $12 million FDOT Complete Streets project finished in 2024 but promised private investment has not materialized
Residents and business owners point to fragmented property ownership and competing city priorities as obstacles
articles.body:
The mural went up in March 2022. A local artist painted it on the side of what used to be a tire shop at Cervantes and N Street, commissioned by the city's Community Redevelopment Agency to signal change was coming. Palm trees. A pelican. The words "West Side Rising" in sunset colors.

Four years later, the tire shop is still empty. The mural has faded. And the stretch of West Cervantes Street between Graffiti Bridge and I-110 looks much the same as it did a decade ago: check-cashing storefronts, overgrown lots, shuttered gas stations with the pumps removed.

"They told us this was going to be the next Palafox," said Denise Williams, who has owned a hair salon near the A Street intersection since 2009. "I'm still waiting."

The money went somewhere

The West Cervantes CRA was established in 2019, designating a 340-acre district as blighted and eligible for tax increment financing. The mechanism captures increases in property tax revenue within the district and funnels it back into redevelopment.

Since fiscal year 2021, the CRA has allocated $4.2 million. According to annual reports reviewed by The Flightline, the largest expenditures include:

  • $1.1 million for streetscape improvements and sidewalk repairs
  • $890,000 for façade grants to existing businesses
  • $650,000 for property acquisition (two parcels, both still vacant)
  • $480,000 for planning studies and consultant contracts
  • $340,000 for the Complete Streets project local match

The façade grants produced visible results. Williams received $15,000 to replace her awning and repaint her building. A barbershop two doors down got new windows. But the larger promise—new construction, mixed-use development, anchor tenants—remains unrealized.

"We've made progress on the infrastructure side," said Marcus Hayes, the CRA's program manager, in an interview last month. "The private investment piece takes longer. You have to change perceptions."

The road got fixed. Then nothing.

The most visible investment came from the Florida Department of Transportation. A $12 million Complete Streets reconstruction of Cervantes from Pace Boulevard to I-110 finished in late 2024. The project narrowed travel lanes, added bike lanes, widened sidewalks and installed new lighting and landscaping.

City officials predicted the redesign would spark development. At a ribbon-cutting ceremony in November 2024, then-Mayor D.C. Reeves called it "the infrastructure that unlocks investment."

Eighteen months later, no new commercial permits have been pulled for properties fronting the reconstructed corridor. The bike lanes sit mostly empty. Three businesses that were open during construction have since closed.

Tom Brennan owns one of the properties that didn't close—a transmission repair shop his father opened in 1987. He's watched the neighborhood's arc for four decades.

"The road's nicer," he said. "But nice roads don't fill buildings. People with money to invest, they look at this area and see problems. They see crime stats. They see the homeless population. A bike lane doesn't fix that."

The ownership puzzle

Part of the challenge is structural. Property records show the corridor's commercial parcels are split among dozens of owners. Some are local families holding lots for decades. Others are out-of-state LLCs that acquired properties during the foreclosure wave following 2008.

The CRA has attempted to assemble parcels for larger development. Its two acquisitions—a former convenience store site and an adjacent vacant lot—were intended as the anchor for a mixed-use project. A 2023 request for proposals drew one response, from a Tallahassee developer who later withdrew.

"The numbers don't work," said Patricia Morrison, a commercial real estate broker who has listed properties in the area. "Construction costs are up 40% since 2020. Rents you can get on West Cervantes don't justify new construction. Not yet."

The CRA has discussed offering additional incentives—gap financing, property tax abatements—but hasn't formalized a program. Hayes said staff capacity is limited. The CRA shares personnel with the city's Housing and Community Development department.

Competing priorities

West Cervantes is one of three active CRAs in Pensacola. The Urban Core CRA, covering downtown and adjacent neighborhoods, commands more attention and resources. Its tax increment is larger—downtown property values have climbed steadily—and its projects are more visible.

Council member Teniadé Broughton, whose District 6 includes much of the West Cervantes corridor, has pushed for more dedicated focus.

"We cannot keep treating west side neighborhoods as afterthoughts," Broughton said at a May budget workshop. "The CRA was supposed to be a tool for equity. Right now it's reinforcing the same patterns."

City Administrator Keith Wilkins said the administration is committed to the corridor but acknowledged competing demands.

"Every dollar we put into West Cervantes is a dollar we're not putting somewhere else," Wilkins said. "We have to be strategic. We have to show results to maintain public support for these tools."

What residents see

On a Tuesday afternoon in late June, traffic on Cervantes moved steadily. The new sidewalks were clean. The landscaping looked maintained.

But the storefronts told a different story. Between Graffiti Bridge and I-110, a stretch of roughly one mile, The Flightline counted 14 vacant commercial buildings and six empty lots. Some had for-sale signs. Some had nothing at all.

At a bus stop near D Street, Robert Coleman waited for the Route 8. He's lived in the Tanyard neighborhood, just north of Cervantes, for 31 years.

"They keep saying development's coming," Coleman said. "But development for who? Because the people who live here, we could use a grocery store. We could use a clinic. What we're going to get, if anything comes, is probably something none of us can afford."

The nearest full-service grocery store is a Winn-Dixie on Mobile Highway, about two miles west. The nearest urgent care clinic is on Ninth Avenue, across I-110.

Williams, the salon owner, said she's stopped going to CRA meetings. She went to several in 2021 and 2022. She doesn't see the point anymore.

"I'll believe it when I see it," she said. "Right now what I see is the same thing I saw 10 years ago. Just with a nicer mural."

The West Cervantes CRA board meets monthly. The next meeting is July 22 at 3 p.m. in City Hall.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's gate traffic is about to get worse. The Navy says that's the point.
articles.dek: New security protocols rolling out this fall will add inspection time at every gate. Base officials say post-2019 changes aren't negotiable. Commuters who cross the base daily aren't so sure.
brief: Enhanced vehicle inspection protocols at NAS Pensacola gates will begin October 1, adding an estimated 3-7 minutes per vehicle during peak hours
The changes stem from ongoing security overhauls following the December 2019 terrorist attack that killed three sailors
Thousands of civilian commuters who use base roads as shortcuts between Gulf Breeze and Pensacola face longer waits or alternate routes
articles.body:
The line at NAS Pensacola's main gate stretched past the Bayou Grande bridge at 7:23 on a Tuesday morning last month. Brake lights blinked in sequence as cars inched toward the guard shack. A woman in a silver Camry checked her phone. The clock on the dashboard read 7:31 when she finally handed her ID to a security officer.

Eight minutes. Not terrible by base standards. But come October, that wait could double.

The Navy announced last week that enhanced vehicle inspection protocols will take effect at all NAS Pensacola access points starting October 1. The changes include expanded random vehicle searches, new under-vehicle scanning equipment at the main and back gates, and revised credentialing procedures for civilian workers and contractors.

Base officials estimate the new protocols will add three to seven minutes per vehicle during morning and afternoon rush periods. For the roughly 23,000 people who pass through NAS Pensacola gates on an average weekday, that math gets uncomfortable fast.

The 2019 shadow

The security expansion isn't arbitrary. It traces directly to December 6, 2019, when a Saudi military trainee opened fire in a classroom building on base, killing Ensign Joshua Watson, Airman Mohammed Haitham, and Airman Apprentice Cameron Walters before being shot by responding deputies.

The attack prompted a sweeping review of security practices across all Navy installations hosting international military students. Some changes came quickly—suspended Saudi training programs, enhanced background screening, restricted personal firearms policies. Others have rolled out incrementally over the past six years.

"We made a commitment to the families of those we lost and to everyone who works and trains here," said Capt. David Wroe, NAS Pensacola's commanding officer, at a press briefing Monday. "These protocols reflect that commitment. They are not negotiable."

Wroe declined to detail specific inspection procedures, citing operational security. But he acknowledged the impact on traffic flow and said the base is adding personnel and lanes to offset delays where possible.

The commuter problem

NAS Pensacola sits on a peninsula that creates a geographic bottleneck between Gulf Breeze and downtown Pensacola. For decades, civilian commuters with base access have used the installation's internal roads as a shortcut, avoiding the congestion on the Pensacola Bay Bridge and Bayou Chico routes.

That shortcut depends on quick gate passage. When waits stretch past ten minutes, the time savings disappear.

Mike Thornton has driven through the base every workday for eleven years. He lives in Tiger Point and works at a law firm on Palafox. The base route saves him twenty minutes compared to the Three Mile Bridge, he said. On a good day.

"I've already noticed it getting slower the last year or so," Thornton said outside the Navy Federal Credit Union on Navy Boulevard last week. "If they're telling me to add another ten minutes to that, I'm probably done. I'll take my chances with the bridge."

The base doesn't track how many pass-through commuters use its roads versus personnel reporting for duty. But anecdotal evidence and rush-hour traffic patterns suggest the number is substantial. A 2018 Naval Facilities Engineering Command study estimated that eliminating commuter pass-through would reduce gate volume by 15 to 20 percent.

That study was conducted before the 2019 attack. Its recommendations were never implemented.

No easy alternatives

For Pensacola-area drivers, the alternatives to base transit are limited and already strained.

The Pensacola Bay Bridge carries roughly 45,000 vehicles daily, according to Florida Department of Transportation counts from 2025. The Three Mile Bridge connecting Gulf Breeze to Pensacola Beach handles another 28,000. Both routes experience significant congestion during commute hours, particularly when weather or accidents create backups.

The long-discussed Pensacola Bay Bridge replacement project remains in design phase, with construction not expected to begin until 2029 at the earliest. A proposed connector route through the former Ellyson Field property has languished in planning limbo for over a decade.

"The infrastructure wasn't built for the population we have now," said Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh at a county meeting last month. "Adding pressure at the base gates just moves the problem somewhere else."

Bergosh said he has requested a meeting with base leadership to discuss traffic mitigation but has not received a response.

Contractor concerns

Defense contractors and civilian workers assigned to NAS Pensacola face a different calculus. They can't choose an alternate route. They have to get on base.

Patricia Womack manages a team of twelve civilian IT specialists who support training operations at the base. Her employees arrive between 6:30 and 8 a.m. depending on shift assignments. She's already reworking schedules to account for October.

"I'm telling my people to plan for an extra half hour," Womack said by phone. "That's unpaid time sitting in their cars. Multiply that by however many contractors work on that base. It adds up."

NAS Pensacola employs approximately 16,000 military personnel and 7,000 civilians across its various commands and tenant activities. The base is the largest single-site employer in the Pensacola metro area.

Womack said she understands the security rationale but wishes the Navy had consulted more with contractor leadership before announcing the timeline.

"We found out the same time everyone else did," she said. "A little advance coordination would have helped."

What happens next

Base officials say they will open additional inspection lanes at the main gate starting September 15 to allow a transition period before full implementation. They are also evaluating extended gate hours at the back gate on Blue Angel Parkway, though no decision has been announced.

The new protocols will apply to all vehicles entering the installation, including those with Department of Defense decals and military ID holders. Random secondary inspections will increase from approximately 5 percent of vehicles to approximately 15 percent, according to base public affairs.

Capt. Wroe said the Navy recognizes the inconvenience but views it as necessary.

"Security and convenience sometimes conflict," he said Monday. "When they do, security wins. Every time."

The woman in the silver Camry—a Navy civilian employee who declined to give her name—had a simpler take when she finally cleared the gate that Tuesday morning.

"I just leave earlier now," she said. "What else can you do?"
